## Calibration accuracy: framing quantization

Analysis from a 2026-07-08 session on the 3900X, prompted by
the framing/sample header value jumping between ~1 ns and
~21 ns across runs while loop/iter held steady at 0.49 ns.

### Observation: framing sits on a ~10 ns lattice

Repeated runs reported framing/sample of 1.02, 11.12, 11.22,
and 21.22 ns — not a continuous drift but discrete steps of
~10.1 ns. Decoding through the two-point fit
(`src/overhead.rs`), the underlying `min_low` measurements
were 50, 60, and 70 ns.

We think the mechanism is TSC granularity: `minstant` reads
the TSC, and on Zen 2 the TSC is derived from the 100 MHz
reference clock, so elapsed-time readings quantize to ~10 ns
steps.

### Why framing wobbles but loop/iter is steady

Both constants come from the same two measurements; they
differ in amortization:

- `framing = min_low - N_LOW * loop_per_iter` — inherits
  `min_low`'s quantization one-for-one (noise amplification
  ~1.01, per the comment in `src/overhead.rs`).
- `loop_per_iter = (min_high - min_low) / 9_900` — the same
  ±1-2 quanta divides by 9,900 → ±0.002 ns, invisible.

Framing is the only quantity in the fit measured
un-amortized; that asymmetry is the whole story.

### The min estimator cannot see inside a quantum

An interval of true length T measures as ⌊T/q⌋ or ⌈T/q⌉
quanta depending on phase alignment; the min over many phase
re-rolls converges to the lower reading. So a min-based
estimate reports the lattice floor and can under-read the
true duration by up to one quantum. The true framing on the
3900X lies somewhere in roughly [1, 11] ns; the 1.02 and
21.22 readings are the floor and ceiling lattice points.
Within one run the phase appears stable (100k samples pick
one quantum); re-entering the measurement re-rolls it.

### Error propagation through `pick_inner`

The framing estimate is load-bearing beyond post-hoc
subtraction — it sizes the experiment
(`src/harness.rs::pick_inner`,
`inner ≈ 10 * framing / step_cost`):

- Auto-sized benches: per-call adjustment error is
  `δ/inner ≈ δ/(10 * framing)` relative to step cost —
  independent of step speed. With framing ≈ 11 ns and δ up
  to a ~10 ns quantum, up to ~9% relative error on every
  auto-sized bench.
- Under-estimated framing under-sizes `inner`: a 1.02 ns
  calibration draw on a ~2.9 ns step picks inner ≈ 4 instead
  of ~43; the true ~11 ns framing is then ~2.8 ns per call
  (~50% apparatus), of which only 0.26 ns is subtracted.
  Nothing in the report reveals it.
- `--inner` override at 1 exposes the full δ (~10-20 ns)
  per call, unamortized.

Consequence: a min-of-mins repeat of the current fit would
be the wrong fix — consistently landing on the *low* quantum
consistently under-sizes `inner`. Over-estimating framing is
harmless (bigger `inner`); under-estimating distorts.

### Fix: amortized framing measurement

Measure the timer-pair cost inside one window: one timer
read at the start, a loop of M back-to-back timer pairs, one
read at the end, divide by M. The ±1-quantum error on the
window amortizes to q/M per pair (~0.001 ns at M = 10,000) —
the same trick that already makes loop/iter steady.

Caveat: this measures the *throughput* cost of paired reads,
which can differ from a timer pair pipelined around real
work. We think it is still a far better subtraction constant
than "somewhere in a 10 ns interval", but it carries a
different (small) bias, not ground truth.

### Frequency dependence: what is constant, what is not

- The TSC rate and its ~10 ns quantum are invariant —
  constant across turbo, throttle, and idle states.
- The framing *cost* is core-clocked work (~tens of cycles
  of `rdtsc` + arithmetic), so its wall-clock value scales
  with core frequency: the same cycles take ~2× longer at a
  2.2 GHz throttle vs 4.6 GHz boost. Same for loop/iter.
- In practice calibration (post-warmup) and benches (hot
  loops) both run boosted, so the constants usually match.
  When frequency does shift, step cost shifts with framing
  cost, so contamination stays roughly proportional rather
  than blowing up; the subtraction just stops being exact.

So a cached calibration is a *machine + frequency-regime*
constant, not a universal one.

### Design: cached calibration in the config file

Store the calibration constants in the existing config file
(`src/config.rs`) rather than measuring fresh each run. The
primary benefit is run-to-run *comparability*, not startup
time: with a pinned adjustment constant, deltas between runs
reflect the bench, not the calibration lottery (~±0.23 ns on
adjusted values at inner = 43 today).

- An explicit calibrate command writes/refreshes the entry;
  runs use it when present, calibrate live otherwise.
- The entry carries provenance: CPU model, iiac-perf
  version, calibration date, raw `min_low`/`min_high`.
- Each run does a quick live amortized framing check
  (milliseconds) against the cached value: within a few
  percent, use the cache silently; off by more (throttle,
  different governor, stale file), warn or fall back to
  live. Cache validity becomes measured, not trusted.
- The report header states which mode adjusted the run —
  cached (with date) vs live — so a report is never
  ambiguous about its constants.

Rejected alternative: scaling calibration length with bench
duration (`-d` percentage). The residual error is
quantization, not sampling depth — more time in one
continuous measurement does not re-roll the phase alignment —
and calibration measures a machine property, not a bench
property.

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

_No cycle currently in progress._

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Amortized framing calibration + cached constants in config
   — framing is quantized to the ~10 ns TSC lattice and the
   estimate sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the
   experiment (up to ~9% relative error, worst case ~50%
   apparatus contamination); measure M timer pairs in one
   window (error q/M), cache in config with provenance +
   live validity check, header says cached vs live
   [analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization)
2. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
3. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
4. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
5. Add framing adjustment to `Probe::report` (subtract
   `Overhead::framing_per_sample_ns` ≈ 11 ns in an `adjusted`
   column, mirroring `harness::print_report`)
6. Convert `harness` / `Bench` to probe-based measurement. Will
   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
7. Rename app
8. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
9. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
   `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
   {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
10. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
    (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
    use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
11. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
12. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly
    (compare to mpsc-1t/2t which use crossbeam under the std API)
13. `tokio-mpsc-1t` / `tokio-mpsc-2t` — `tokio::sync::mpsc` round-trip
    inside a Tokio runtime (async overhead)
14. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
15. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path
16. When the second channel impl lands, extract shared message types
    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
17. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
18. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.

## Done

Completed tasks are moved from `## Todo` to here, `## Done`, as they are completed
and older `## Done` sections are moved to [done.md](done.md) to keep this file small.

content.text:
Good data to reason from — the series shows exactly why a trimmed row would help, and also which trim to pick.

**What your numbers say.** The distribution is strongly multi-modal: ~1% of handoffs land at ~200 ns, ~9% smear from 0.25–3.6 µs, then a heavy plateau at ~3.7–5.5 µs, and a 1% tail out to ~400 µs. Comparing across your six runs:

- full `mean`: 4,815 / 4,914 / 4,826 / 4,896 / 4,789 / 4,925 ns — wobbles ~±1.4%, and `mean min-p99` wobbles just as much. The wobble isn't noise in the plateau; it's the *mode mix* (how many samples fall in the fast p1–p10 smear) shifting run to run.
- the plateau center (p50–p60 band mean): 5,378 / 5,392 / 5,392 / 5,398 / 5,398 / 5,402 ns — stable to ~±0.2%.

So a core-trimmed statistic is the run-to-run-comparable number for this bench, much more so than the full mean. That's the same comparability motivation as the cached calibration.

**p10–p90 vs p40–p60.** I'd pick **p10–p90** (interdecile mean/stdev — a standard 10% trimmed mean):

- `mean p40-p60` is essentially a robust median — informative, but it collapses to one number you can already eyeball as the p50 boundary; and its stdev would mostly measure band/lattice quantization, not the workload.
- `p10-p90` keeps enough mass (80%) that its stdev still describes the core spread, while excluding both the fast-mode smear and the tail. In your data it would sit ~5.0–5.1 µs with a small stdev, and should be far steadier than `min-p99` (which keeps the whole p1–p10 smear — that's why it didn't stabilize anything).

One caution: for multi-modal data like this, the trimmed row *hides real behavior* — those fast handoffs are presumably genuine (consumer already waiting vs. batched wakeups), not measurement error. So it should be an additional row beside `mean`/`mean min-p99`, never a replacement — and maybe the trim bounds belong in config/flag (`--trim p10:p90`?) rather than hardcoded, since the right core band is bench-shaped.

Want me to add it as a `## Todo` entry — something like "Trimmed core stats: `mean/stdev p10-p90` row (configurable trim bounds)" ranked after unit scaling, with a pointer back to this series as the motivating data? It fits naturally into the report-options family alongside unit scaling and `--decimals`. (I'd keep the current calibration cycle rolling rather than detour into it now.)

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

Framing is measured un-amortized, so it inherits the full
~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization):
measure M timer pairs in one window (error q/M), cache the
constants in the config file with provenance + a live validity
check, and say cached vs live in the report header. Calibration
banner values print at 3 decimals always (sub-ns resolution is
the point; `--decimals` remains the report-table knob).

- 0.21.0-0 chore: open cached-calibration cycle (current)
- 0.21.0-1 feat: amortized framing calibration
- 0.21.0-2 feat: calibrate command + config cache
- 0.21.0-3 feat: cached calibration + validity check
- 0.21.0 close-out

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
2. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
3. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
4. Add framing adjustment to `Probe::report` (subtract
   `Overhead::framing_per_sample_ns` ≈ 11 ns in an `adjusted`
   column, mirroring `harness::print_report`)
5. Convert `harness` / `Bench` to probe-based measurement. Will
   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
6. Rename app
7. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
8. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
   `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
   {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
9. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
   (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
   use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
10. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
11. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly
    (compare to mpsc-1t/2t which use crossbeam under the std API)
12. `tokio-mpsc-1t` / `tokio-mpsc-2t` — `tokio::sync::mpsc` round-trip
    inside a Tokio runtime (async overhead)
13. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
14. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path
15. When the second channel impl lands, extract shared message types
    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
16. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
17. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.

and older `## Done` sections are moved to [done.md](done.md) to keep this file small.

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization):
measure M timer pairs in one window (error q/M), cache the
constants in the config file with provenance + a live validity
check, and say cached vs live in the report header. Calibration
banner values print at 3 decimals always (sub-ns resolution is
the point; `--decimals` remains the report-table knob).

- 0.21.0-1 feat: amortized framing calibration
- 0.21.0-2 feat: calibrate command + config cache
- 0.21.0-3 feat: cached calibration + validity check
- 0.21.0 close-out

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
2. Trimmed core stats: `mean/stdev p10-p90` report row,
   additional to (never replacing) `mean` / `mean min-p99`;
   trim bounds possibly configurable (`--trim p10:p90`?) —
   the full mean wobbles ~±1.4% with the run's mode mix while
   the core plateau is ~±0.2% stable, so the trimmed row is
   the run-to-run comparable number [[57]]
3. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
4. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
5. Add framing adjustment to `Probe::report` (subtract
   `Overhead::framing_per_sample_ns` ≈ 11 ns in an `adjusted`
   column, mirroring `harness::print_report`)
6. Convert `harness` / `Bench` to probe-based measurement. Will
   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
7. Rename app
8. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
9. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
   `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
   {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
10. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
    (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
    use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
11. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
12. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly

13. `tokio-mpsc-1t` / `tokio-mpsc-2t` — `tokio::sync::mpsc` round-trip

14. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
15. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path

    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
17. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
18. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.

  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only

  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates

Both experiments are in, and the data flips part of the design on its head — I want your input before committing. Warm, back-to-back runs:

| shape | framing result | stability |
|---|---|---|
| old min-based intercept (0.20.1) | 0.00–8.82 ns (this cycle's motivation) | ±full quantum, clamps at 0 |
| design.md's back-to-back pairs | 46.3–50.8 ns | ~±5% (tracks core clock) |
| amortized two-point windows | 53.62 / 53.64 / 48.2 ns | ±0.02 ns warm back-to-back |

**The amortization works beautifully — but both amortized shapes measure a different quantity than the one we subtract.** A window necessarily times *call-to-call*: the full ~50 ns cost of two clock reads lands inside it. But a recorded sample only contains what happens *between the two clock reads* — the vDSO read latency itself sits mostly outside the measured interval, and the CPU overlaps the rest with the inner loop. That between-reads slice is the ~1–11 ns the old intercept measured (correct quantity, hopelessly quantized). The ~40 ns gap between the two isn't small bias — subtracting the 50 ns figure would over-adjust every auto-sized bench by a few percent. And the between-reads slice is, as far as I can see, *not measurable by any window trick* — amortizing it turns it into the full cost by construction.

**But here's the out:** the two constants have different jobs, per design.md's own error analysis:

- **`pick_inner` sizing** was the real harm (a low framing draw → tiny `inner` → up to ~50% contamination). Sizing wants a *stable, conservative* constant — the amortized ~50 ns is ideal: rock-steady, and over-estimating framing only makes `inner` bigger (design.md: harmless).
- **Subtraction** wants the between-reads constant. Keep the min-based intercept for it, quantized as ever — but once `inner` is sized off the amortized constant, `inner` grows ~5×, and the subtraction's worst-case error `q/inner` drops to ~2% of step cost. The quantization stops mattering because it's divided by a properly-sized `inner`.

So my recommendation: **carry both constants** — `framing_call_ns` (amortized two-point, drives sizing, the stable number the banner and config cache feature) and `framing_sample_ns` (min-based intercept, drives subtraction, banner-annotated as quantized ±q). That solves the original under-sizing problem completely, avoids over-subtraction, and gives the cache/validity-check a stable constant to validate against. It does mean design.md's "Fix" section needs a follow-up subsection recording that its proposed measurement measures call-to-call cost, and the two-constant resolution.

content.text:
Let me explain the terms first, then get the r5-7600x data, then give my read on not subtracting.

## Framing vs sampling

**A sample** is one recorded measurement. In the harness a sample is:

```
start = Instant::now();      // clock read A
for _ in 0..inner { step() } // the workload, inner iterations
start.elapsed()              // clock read B → sample = B − A
```

The sample (divided by `inner`) is the per-call estimate that lands in the histogram. "Sampling" is just taking many of these.

**Framing** is this project's name (coined in `overhead.rs`; the industry usually says *timer overhead* or *measurement overhead*) for the cost of the timer pair that *frames* the workload — like a picture frame around the inner loop. It's a per-sample constant, which is why `inner` amortizes it. What this week's experiments exposed is that "the cost of the timer pair" is two different numbers depending on where you stand:

- **In-interval framing (~1–11 ns here)** — what actually lands *inside* `B − A`: the tail of `now()` after it reads the clock, loop entry, and `elapsed()`'s prologue up to its clock read. The clock reads themselves sit mostly *outside* the interval (work before read A and after read B doesn't count), and out-of-order execution overlaps much of the rest with the workload. This is the quantity subtraction wants — and it's the one we can only measure through a quantized min, because any window trick that brackets many pairs necessarily converts it into…
- **Call-to-call framing (~50 ns here)** — the *full* apparatus cost of a sample: both vDSO clock-read latencies, call overhead, everything. This is what throughput sees, it's what my amortized windows measure to ±0.02 ns, and it's the right constant for *sizing* (`pick_inner`) and duration budgeting — but subtracting it over-corrects, because most of it was never inside the recorded interval.

Links: [std::time::Instant](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.Instant.html) (wraps `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`), [clock_gettime(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clock_gettime.2.html) and [vdso(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/vdso.7.html) (why a read is ~20 ns with no syscall), [criterion's analysis chapter](https://bheisler.github.io/criterion.rs/book/analysis.html) (the same batch-and-divide amortization), Intel's Paoloni whitepaper ["How to Benchmark Code Execution Times on Intel IA-32/IA-64"](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/white-papers/ia-32-ia-64-benchmark-code-execution-paper.pdf) (the classic on timer-read overhead and serialization), and our own [design.md analysis](notes/design.md).

content.text:
Here's the r5-7600x data (cold first run after 30 s idle, then 5 warm back-to-back):

| estimator | cold | warm ×5 | warm stability |
|---|---|---|---|
| min-based intercept (old, computed from raws) | 0.2 ns | 3.3 / 4.5 / 4.5 / 4.5 / 4.5 ns | ±quantum, the known wobble |
| back-to-back pairs | 36.357 | **32.355 ×5 identical** | < 0.001 ns |
| amortized two-point windows | 25.703 | 23.071 / 23.069 / 22.890 / 23.069 / 23.069 | ~±0.1% |

You're right about this machine — it's a far better measurement box (the desktop 3900X gave ±5% between warm runs; here the back-to-back number repeats to the third decimal). Two things worth noting: the cold penalty is only ~11% on the amortized constants (vs. the 0-vs-3.3 chaos of the intercept), and on this machine the two-point window (23.1 ns) comes out *below* back-to-back (32.4 ns) — the inner loop lets the CPU overlap the clock reads with work, so the two-point number is the marginal per-sample cost in the *real sample shape*. That makes it the best sizing constant, and it's stable.

**On not subtracting — I read it the same way, with one refinement.** The adjustment currently subtracts two constants of very different quality:

- `framing/inner` — the in-interval framing. We genuinely cannot produce this number: it's quantized ±10 ns and unamortizable by construction. Subtracting a guess dressed as 3 decimals is false precision. **Drop it.**
- `loop_per_iter` — the amortized slope, 0.3686 ±0.0001 ns on this box, and it's the *dominant* apparatus term per call anyway (0.37 ns vs framing's ~4 ns/inner≈40 ≈ 0.1 ns). This one is a good number. **Keep it.**

Then the stable amortized call-cost (~23 ns) takes over `pick_inner` sizing — which was the actual harm in the design.md error analysis (a 0.00 draw under-sizing `inner`). With `inner` sized off a conservative, stable 23 ns instead of a quantized 0–9 ns draw, the *unsubtracted* in-interval framing residue that stays in the reported values is bounded to roughly 1–2% of step cost — and the report can state that bound honestly instead of pretending to remove it.

So the revised -1 scope would be: amortized two-point calibration (slope + call-cost, both stable) · framing subtraction removed from `adjusted` (loop/iter still subtracted) · `pick_inner` sizes from call-cost · banner reports `frame/sample (call-to-call)` at 3 decimals · design.md gets a subsection recording the in-interval vs call-to-call distinction and why subtraction of the former is unmeasurable. The `-2`/`-3` cache steps then cache constants that are actually stable, which makes the validity check meaningful.

Shall I rework the code to that design?

Let me take those one at a time, in plainer terms — then I'll capture it in design.md.

**Your understanding, slightly refined.** You have the jump mechanism right: the clock readout moves in ~10 ns steps, and where your measurement starts *within* a step (the phase) decides whether a given true duration reads low or high. Within one run the phase stays put — every sample rounds the same way — so the whole run commits to one lattice point; the next run re-rolls and lands 10 ns away. The refinement: this only poisons the **per-sample (framing) constant**, not the inner-loop constant, because of how each is computed:

- framing comes from *one un-amortized number* (`min_low` ≈ 40 ns, minus the loop's share) — a ±10 ns roll on a ~40 ns number is the whole estimate. That's your 0.00 ↔ 3.27 jump.
- loop/iter comes from a *difference divided by 9,900* — the same ±10 ns becomes ±0.001 ns. That's why it never jumps.

So "sampling error is high" is true specifically for the un-amortized point; anything we can divide by a big N is fine.

**What I was trying to say with the two framings** — a timeline of one sample:

```
--- now() ----------- inner loop ----------- elapsed() ---
  ↑ clock read A                          ↑ clock read B
        |<——— the sample = B − A ————————>|
```

The two clock calls cost ~30 ns total, but most of that cost sits *before read A* and *after read B* — outside the sample. Only a small sliver (~1–10 ns) lands inside `B − A`. Subtraction wants the sliver, and the sliver is exactly the thing stuck behind the 10 ns granularity — any amortized window wraps *whole calls*, so it measures the full ~23–32 ns instead. Precise number, wrong quantity. That's the whole tension: **the number we can measure well isn't the number we'd subtract, and the number we'd subtract can't be measured well.** Hence my lean to your instinct: stop subtracting it.

**The producer/consumer consistency is an identity, not a coincidence.** Each thread's probe intervals run back-to-back, so they *tile* the run's wall-clock time. Both threads span the same wall time and record the same count (every handoff appears once in each). Therefore:

```
mean = (sum of intervals) / count ≈ wall_time / count   — same for both
```

Check against your earlier 5 s run: 5.0 s ÷ 1,035,886 = 4,827 ns; reported means were 4,814.6 (p) and 4,813.9 (c) — the identity, minus a small per-iteration gap. The distributions of p and c differ (their stdevs disagree by a few ns), but their means are pinned to the same throughput ratio. `min-p99` trims a same-sized 1% tail from each, so it inherits most of the identity — that's your 4,778.487 vs 4,778.378. The 65 ns shift *between* runs is a real throughput change (~1.4%), the mode-mix wobble from the trimmed-stats note. Sharp consequence: **on a closed-loop bench the untrimmed mean is a throughput number, not a latency-shape number** — which strengthens the p10–p90 row idea.

## Timer overhead: in-interval vs call-to-call

Analysis from a 2026-07-13 session (3900X + r5-7600x),
prompted by implementing the amortized framing fix above: the
amortized measurement came out 5-10x larger than the intercept
fit it replaced (3900X: ~50 ns vs 1-21 ns; r5-7600x: ~23-32 ns
vs 0-4.5 ns). Both are "the cost of the timer pair" — they
measure different slices of it.

A sample is `now()` (clock read A) ... inner loop ...
`elapsed()` (clock read B); the recorded value is B - A. The
two timer calls cost ~23-50 ns in total, but most of that
sits *before read A* and *after read B* — outside the
recorded interval. Only a small sliver lands inside B - A.

- **In-interval overhead** (~1-11 ns) — the sliver: `now()`'s
  tail after read A, loop entry, `elapsed()`'s prologue up to
  read B; out-of-order execution overlaps much of it with the
  workload. This is what subtraction would want to remove
  from a sample.
- **Call-to-call overhead** (~23-50 ns) — the full apparatus
  cost of taking a sample, both clock-read latencies
  included. This is what throughput sees, and what sizing
  (`pick_inner`) and duration budgeting care about.

The measurability is asymmetric, and unfavorably so:

- Call-to-call amortizes: a window around M whole samples
  contains every bit of the pair cost, so q/M quantization →
  measured to ±0.02 ns warm (r5-7600x: 32.355 ns back-to-back
  pairs, identical across 5 runs; 23.07 ns in the two-point
  window shape, ±0.1%).
- In-interval cannot amortize *by construction*: any window
  wraps whole calls and thus measures call-to-call. The only
  estimator is the un-amortized min (the intercept fit), stuck
  at ±one ~10 ns quantum — on a ~1-11 ns quantity.

So the number we can measure precisely is not the number
subtraction wants, and the number subtraction wants cannot be
measured precisely. Consequences (0.21.0 cycle direction):

- Drop the framing term from the `adjusted` column — a
  quantized guess rendered at 3 decimals is false precision.
  Keep the loop/iter term: the amortized slope is measured to
  ±0.001 ns and dominates the per-call apparatus cost anyway.
- Size `inner` from the *call-to-call* constant: stable,
  conservative (over-sizing is harmless), and it removes the
  original harm — a low quantized framing draw under-sizing
  the experiment. The unsubtracted in-interval residue is then
  bounded by ~q/inner, roughly 1-2% of step cost, and can be
  stated as a bound instead of pretended away.
- The two-point window shape (M whole samples per window at
  N_LOW / N_HIGH) is the right call-to-call estimator: it
  keeps the real sample's pipelining context. We think this is
  why it reads lower than bare back-to-back pairs on r5-7600x
  (23.07 vs 32.36 ns — the loop gives the reads work to
  overlap with).

## Closed-loop mean identity

Why producer and consumer full means (and near enough their
min-p99 trimmed means) agree to ~0.1 ns within a run while
moving ~1.4% between runs (observed on r5-7600x tp-pc,
2026-07-13).

Each thread's probe intervals run back-to-back, so they tile
the run's wall-clock span. Both threads span the same wall
time and record the same count (every handoff appears once in
each thread's series), so:

    mean = sum(intervals) / count ≈ wall_time / count

- Same wall time, same count → same mean, for *any* two
  distributions of the same closed loop. Check: a 5 s tp-pc
  run recorded count = 1,035,886; 5.0 s / 1,035,886 =
  4,827 ns vs reported means 4,814.6 (p) / 4,813.9 (c) — the
  identity minus the small per-iteration gap outside the
  probe.
- `min-p99` trims a same-sized 1% tail from each side's
  series, so it inherits most of the identity (4,778.487 vs
  4,778.378 ns).
- Consequence: on a closed-loop bench the untrimmed mean is a
  *throughput* number, not a latency-shape number. Run-to-run
  mean shifts are real throughput changes (the mode-mix
  wobble), which is the case for the trimmed core stats row
  (see chores-04
  [Trimmed core stats](chores/chores-04.md#trimmed-core-stats-p10-p90)).

cat >> notes/design.md << 'EOF'

## Comparing implementations: least significant change

How to decide whether implementation A is really faster than B
at 95% confidence, worked from a six-run tp-pc series on
r5-7600x (2026-07-13).

The unit of replication is the **run**, not the sample. A run's
millions of samples make its within-run standard error
microscopic; what dominates comparison error is run-to-run
systematic drift (mode mix, frequency regime, calibration).
So compare per-run statistics:

- Do n runs of A and n of B, **interleaved** (A,B,A,B,...) so
  thermal / frequency drift hits both arms alike; same machine,
  same duration, same pinning; discard an initial warm-up run.
- Take one statistic per run (today `mean min-p99`; the
  trimmed p10-p90 row when it lands), giving n values per arm.
- Two-sample t at 95%: LSC = t(0.975, 2n-2) * s * sqrt(2/n),
  with s the pooled run-to-run stdev of the statistic.

From the observed series (`mean min-p99`: 4752.5, 4852.1,
4763.7, 4834.0, 4726.6, 4863.2 ns → s ≈ 58 ns ≈ 1.2%):

- n=3 → LSC ≈ 131 ns (~2.7%)
- n=5 → LSC ≈ 85 ns (~1.8%)
- n=10 → LSC ≈ 55 ns (~1.1%)

Reducing s beats raising n (LSC shrinks only as 1/sqrt(n)):

- A statistic that ignores the mode-mix wobble — the p10-p90
  trimmed mean's observed run-to-run spread was ~±0.2%, putting
  a 5-run LSC near 0.4%.
- A pinned frequency regime (`performance` governor on the
  bench box) and cached calibration constants (this cycle)
  remove two more run-to-run variables.
- A headless idle machine: r5-7600x repeats warm calibration
  constants to ±0.02%; the desktop 3900X wobbles ~±5%.
EOF

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

Framing is measured un-amortized, so it inherits the full
~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization):
measure M timer pairs in one window (error q/M), cache the
constants in the config file with provenance + a live validity
check, and say cached vs live in the report header. Calibration
banner values print at 3 decimals always (sub-ns resolution is
the point; `--decimals` remains the report-table knob).

- 0.21.0-0 chore: open cached-calibration cycle (done)
- 0.21.0-1 feat: amortized framing calibration (current)
- 0.21.0-2 feat: calibrate command + config cache
- 0.21.0-3 feat: cached calibration + validity check
- 0.21.0 close-out

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Use the
[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
2. Trimmed core stats: `mean/stdev p10-p90` report row,
   additional to (never replacing) `mean` / `mean min-p99`;
   trim bounds possibly configurable (`--trim p10:p90`?) —
   the full mean wobbles ~±1.4% with the run's mode mix while
   the core plateau is ~±0.2% stable, so the trimmed row is
   the run-to-run comparable number [[57]]
3. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
4. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
5. Add framing adjustment to `Probe::report` (subtract
   `Overhead::framing_per_sample_ns` ≈ 11 ns in an `adjusted`
   column, mirroring `harness::print_report`)
6. Convert `harness` / `Bench` to probe-based measurement. Will
   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
7. Rename app
8. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
9. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
   `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
   {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
10. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
    (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
    use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
11. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
12. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly
    (compare to mpsc-1t/2t which use crossbeam under the std API)

14. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
15. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path
16. When the second channel impl lands, extract shared message types
    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
17. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
18. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

Framing is measured un-amortized, so it inherits the full
~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization):
measure M timer pairs in one window (error q/M), cache the
constants in the config file with provenance + a live validity
check, and say cached vs live in the report header. Calibration
banner values print at 3 decimals always (sub-ns resolution is
the point; `--decimals` remains the report-table knob).

- 0.21.0-0 chore: open cached-calibration cycle (done)
- 0.21.0-1 feat: amortized framing calibration (current)
- 0.21.0-2 feat: calibrate command + config cache
- 0.21.0-3 feat: cached calibration + validity check
- 0.21.0 close-out

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run notes/todo.md` to renumber.
The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
number. Use the

detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
subsections (link via `[N]` ref).

1. Unit scaling in report columns (`us`/`ms`) — per-row
   auto-scale so columns stay eyeball-comparable (bands are
   monotonic, so a row's first/last/mean share a magnitude),
   or `--units ns|auto` for script-stable output; needs
   `--decimals` landed first (`3.18 ms` vs `3 ms`); candidate
   `-4` for the report-options cycle.
2. Trimmed core stats: `mean/stdev p10-p90` report row,
   additional to (never replacing) `mean` / `mean min-p99`;
   trim bounds possibly configurable (`--trim p10:p90`?) —
   the full mean wobbles ~±1.4% with the run's mode mix while
   the core plateau is ~±0.2% stable, so the trimmed row is
   the run-to-run comparable number [[57]]
3. docs: README "Comparing implementations" section — surface
   the LSC / 95%-confidence method (interleaved runs, per-run
   statistic, two-sample t) for users; content in
   [design.md](design.md#comparing-implementations-least-significant-change)
4. Investigate: suspend gap missing from samples. A 0.13.5
   `--no-inhibit` suspend test detected ~1.2 s suspended inside
   the measured window but the max sample was only 4.0 ms,
   while the 0.13.1 test (8.4 s gap) showed the expected 10.4 s
   max sample. We think minstant's TSC may halt across some
   suspends and count through others. Repeat the test comparing
   detected gap vs max sample; if the TSC halts, per-sample
   timing silently loses suspend time — document either way.
5. CLAUDE.md governance model (design cogitation) [20]
6. Add framing adjustment to `Probe::report` (subtract
   `Overhead::framing_per_sample_ns` ≈ 11 ns in an `adjusted`
   column, mirroring `harness::print_report`)

   likely need inner-loop support on `Probe` (batch N calls per
   sample; report divides by N and accounts for per-sample
   framing) so very-small workloads can still amortize timer
   overhead the way `run_adaptive` does today.
8. Rename app
9. Design an app to measure IIAC perforanace written in Rust[1]
10. `ice-ps-2t-wait` — iceoryx2 pub/sub with blocking waits via
    `Listener`/`Notifier` events; completes the {transport} ×
    {wait policy} matrix cell that compares against `mpsc-2t`
11. Switch ice benches to the loan-based zero-copy send path
    (`loan_uninit` + `send`) — the API a perf-sensitive user would
    use, and closer to iceoryx2's own benchmark method
12. Payload-size sweep for the round-trip benches (8 B / 8 KiB /
    1 MiB) — makes iceoryx2's size-independent latency vs channel
    copy cost visible in our own tables
13. `crossbeam-1t` / `crossbeam-2t` — `crossbeam-channel` directly
    (compare to mpsc-1t/2t which use crossbeam under the std API)
14. `tokio-mpsc-1t` / `tokio-mpsc-2t` — `tokio::sync::mpsc` round-trip
    inside a Tokio runtime (async overhead)
15. `flume-1t` / `flume-2t` — `flume` MPMC channel
16. Function-call baselines: direct call vs `Box<dyn Trait>` vs
    `async fn` (poll-once) — anchors the channel/serde numbers
    against the cheapest possible "send a value then receive it" path
17. When the second channel impl lands, extract shared message types
    + round-trip helpers into `src/benches/common.rs` (deferred from 0.2.0)
18. Additional thread control (count, per-thread pin lists, NUMA) —
    shape once a concrete bench needs it
19. Rename crate `iiac-perf` → general-purpose name (breaking; deferred)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.

## Done

Completed tasks are moved from `## Todo` to here, `## Done`, as they are completed
and older `## Done` sections are moved to [done.md](done.md) to keep this file small.

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

Framing is measured un-amortized, so it inherits the full
~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization),
revised mid-cycle by the in-interval vs call-to-call finding
([analysis](design.md#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call)):
amortized two-point window calibration (error q/M on both
points) yields `frame_call_ns` (sizes `inner`; never
subtracted) and `loop_per_iter_ns` (the only subtraction);
cache the constants in the config file with provenance + a
live validity check, and say cached vs live in the report
header. Calibration banner values print at 3 decimals always
(sub-ns resolution is the point; `--decimals` remains the
report-table knob).

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 → 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered

  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes

    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.

    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.

    the current single package, not lock isolation.

    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts

file.content:
# iiac-perf

A general-purpose latency microbenchmark harness for Rust. Each
bench runs against a wall-clock time budget with auto-sized loop
counts, reports a percentile-band histogram in nanoseconds, and
subtracts calibrated apparatus overhead (timer-pair framing +
loop-per-iter) so the output reflects the workload, not the
measurement loop.

Highlights:

- Time-based runs (`-d SECONDS` per bench, `-D SECONDS` total)
  with auto-sized outer/inner loop counts.
- Band-based histogram (min→p1, p1→p10, …, p99→max) with count,
  mean, range, and an adjusted-mean column.
- Per-thread CPU pinning (`--pin`) with independent calibration
  pinning (`--no-pin-cal`), so the cal environment stays stable
  regardless of where bench threads land.
- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
  registering in `src/benches/`.

counts, reports a percentile-band histogram in nanoseconds, and
subtracts calibrated apparatus overhead (the amortized
loop-per-iter cost; the timer-pair cost instead sizes the inner
loop so its residue stays negligible) so the output reflects
the workload, not the measurement loop.

in design.md you say:
- n=3 → LSC ≈ 131 ns (~2.7%)
- n=5 → LSC ≈ 85 ns (~1.8%)
- n=10 → LSC ≈ 55 ns (~1.1%)

What is "n" in "n=x"?

Also a hair brained idea, what if we sleep a random number of microsecs
between each inner loop to try to decouple our measurements from getting
stuck in the sample window?

content.text:
**"n" = the number of runs of *each* implementation** — n=5 means 5 runs of A and 5 runs of B, 10 runs total, interleaved. The table's LSC is the smallest A−B difference in the per-run statistic that clears 95% confidence at that replication. I'll make the doc say that explicitly.

**The idea is not hair-brained at all — it has a name: dithering**, and it's standard practice in ADC/signal-processing land (inject randomness before a quantizer so the quantization error becomes zero-mean noise that averages away instead of a stuck systematic offset). Your diagnosis is exactly right: the problem is that a run's samples all start at the same phase relative to the ~10 ns clock lattice, so the whole run commits to one lattice point ("stuck in the window"). Randomizing the start phase makes each sample independently round low or high in proportion to the true fractional part — the *mean* over many samples then converges to the true value with error shrinking as 1/√N, right through the quantum.

Two refinements to make it work:

- **Random spin, not sleep.** The dither only needs to span one quantum (~10 ns), and it must be fine-grained: a random 0–q delay via a short spin loop (e.g. spin on `rdtsc`, which ticks at ~0.2–0.3 ns) between samples. A `usleep`-style sleep is µs-coarse, costs a syscall, and — worse — wakes on kernel timer boundaries, which can *re-align* the phase instead of randomizing it.
- **It sharpens means, not mins/percentiles.** A dithered min still converges to the lattice floor, and each individual sample stays ±q. So it doesn't help band boundaries — but it makes mean-based aggregate statistics sub-quantum accurate.

And there's a bonus that makes this more than a comparability tweak: a dithered *mean-based* estimator could measure the **in-interval framing** I called unmeasurable — dither the phase of the old two-point measurement, use means instead of mins, and the intercept comes out sub-quantum without any window trick. That would reopen the door to a defensible framing subtraction someday. Capturing both:

cat >> notes/design.md << 'EOF'

## Dithering: random phase injection

Idea from a 2026-07-13 session: insert a random delay between
samples so consecutive measurements stop sharing their phase
relative to the ~10 ns clock lattice ("the whole run commits to
one lattice point"). This is classic **dither** from
signal processing / ADC practice: randomness injected before a
quantizer turns quantization error from a stuck systematic
offset into zero-mean noise that averages away — a mean over N
dithered samples converges through the quantum with error
~q/sqrt(N).

- The dither must be **sub-quantum and fine-grained**: a random
  0..q (~0-10 ns) spin between samples, e.g. spinning on the
  TSC (~0.2-0.3 ns granularity). Not a sleep: `usleep` is
  µs-coarse, costs a syscall, and wakes on kernel timer
  boundaries, which can *re-align* phase rather than randomize
  it. The spin sits outside the timed interval, so it costs
  throughput only, not accuracy.
- Sharpens **means, not mins or percentiles**: a dithered min
  still converges to the lattice floor, and each individual
  sample stays ±q. Band boundaries don't benefit; aggregate
  mean statistics do.
- Possible payoff: a dithered *mean-based* two-point fit could
  estimate the **in-interval framing** to sub-quantum accuracy
  — the quantity
  [call-to-call windows cannot reach](#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call)
  — potentially reviving a defensible framing subtraction.
  Unvalidated; would need an experiment showing the dithered
  intercept is stable run-to-run.
EOF

attachment.snippet:
1	# Design
2	
3	Durable design analyses for iiac-perf. Chores sections record
4	what landed per commit; this file holds the analysis and
5	reasoning that should outlive any one cycle — measurement
6	theory, error models, and the design decisions they drive.
7	Chores and todo entries link here rather than restating.
8	
9	## Architecture Overview
10	
11	iiac-perf is a latency microbenchmark harness: a single binary
12	that runs named benches (mostly inter-thread communication
13	round-trips) and renders each as a band-table latency
14	histogram. The architecture has four layers — startup /
15	environment control, measurement, benches, and reporting.
16	
17	### Startup and environment control
18	
19	`main.rs` runs a fixed pipeline before any bench executes:
20	
21	- **CLI** (clap) — bench selection by exact name or prefix
22	  (`zcr` runs every `zcr-*` bench), plus duration, outer/inner
23	  overrides, pinning, and report options.
24	- **Sleep inhibition** (`inhibit.rs`) — re-exec the process
25	  under `systemd-inhibit` so an idle suspend can't poison a
26	  long run; harness suspend detection remains the backstop.
27	- **Layered config** (`config.rs`) — built-in < XDG file <
28	  project-local file < CLI. Holds defaults and named pin
29	  profiles; the banner reports which files loaded.
30	- **Pinning** (`pin.rs`) — `--pin` core specs / profiles;
31	  main is pinned to a stable core for calibration by default
32	  and the pre-cal affinity restored afterwards, so the cal
33	  pin doesn't leak into the scheduler's bench placement.
34	- **Calibration** (`overhead.rs`) — the two-point fit that
35	  produces the `Overhead` constants (framing/sample,
36	  loop/iter) used for adjustment; see
37	  [Calibration accuracy](#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization).
38	
39	### Measurement
40	
41	Two styles coexist, one harness-driven and one self-driven:
42	
43	- **Harness-driven** (`harness.rs`) — a bench implements the
44	  `Bench` trait (`step()` = one measured operation). The
45	  driver estimates step cost, auto-sizes `inner` so framing
46	  stays ≤~10% of a sample window (`pick_inner`), then times
47	  `inner` back-to-back calls per sample into an HDR
48	  histogram, recording in ps so sub-ns per-call values
49	  survive the divide. Reported values subtract
50	  `Overhead::per_call_ns(inner)`.
51	- **Probe-driven** — for benches whose threads drive
52	  themselves (actor-style), probes are the measurement
53	  channel and there is no outer `Bench` loop:
54	  - `Probe` (`probe.rs`) — caller-timed ns deltas into a
55	    named histogram.
56	  - `TProbe` (`tprobe.rs`) — same shape but records raw
57	    hardware tick deltas (no tick→ns mul-shift on the hot
58	    path); conversion deferred to report time.
59	  - `TProbe2` (`tprobe2.rs`) — scope API: `start(site)`
60	    returns an id, `end(id)` appends a record; records are
61	    drained into the histogram lazily at report time.
62	  - `ticks.rs` — arch-neutral fixed-rate counter facade
63	    (`read_ticks` / `ticks_per_ns`) over per-arch impls
64	    (x86 TSC with CPUID invariant-TSC gate, aarch64 cntvct).
65	
66	Timing sources: harness and `Probe` use `minstant` (TSC-backed
67	`Instant`); `TProbe`/`TProbe2` read ticks directly.
68	
69	### Benches
70	
71	`benches/mod.rs` is a flat registry: each bench module exposes
72	`NAME` and `run`, and registration is appending to `REGISTRY`.
73	Families: timer call-cost baselines (`std-now`, `min-now`),
74	std mpsc round-trips (1t/2t/spin), zc-ring-x1 SPSC/MPSC
75	round-trips (`zcr-*`), iceoryx2 pub/sub and request/response
76	(`ice-*`), and probe-instrumented variants (`probe-mpsc-2t`,
77	`producer-consumer`, `tp-pc`, `tp2-pc`) used to measure the
78	probes themselves. The 1t/2t naming is a convention: same transport,
79	same-thread vs cross-thread, so apparatus and contention
80	effects separate.
81	
82	### Reporting
83	
84	- `bands.rs` — single source of truth for the band ladder
85	  (deciles in the body, zeros/nines tails z4..n10) and label
86	  styles; pinned by tests against the README's table.
87	- `harness::print_report` — the main per-bench table:
88	  first/last/range/count/mean per band plus adjusted column
89	  and whole-vs-trimmed mean/stdev summary lines.
90	- `band_table.rs` — shared renderer for tick-valued probe
91	  histograms, so `TProbe`/`TProbe2` output matches the main
92	  table's shape and columns line up under the bench report.
93	
94	## Calibration accuracy: framing quantization
95	
96	Analysis from a 2026-07-08 session on the 3900X, prompted by
97	the framing/sample header value jumping between ~1 ns and
98	~21 ns across runs while loop/iter held steady at 0.49 ns.
99	
100	### Observation: framing sits on a ~10 ns lattice
101	
102	Repeated runs reported framing/sample of 1.02, 11.12, 11.22,
103	and 21.22 ns — not a continuous drift but discrete steps of
104	~10.1 ns. Decoding through the two-point fit
105	(`src/overhead.rs`), the underlying `min_low` measurements
106	were 50, 60, and 70 ns.
107	
108	We think the mechanism is TSC granularity: `minstant` reads
109	the TSC, and on Zen 2 the TSC is derived from the 100 MHz
110	reference clock, so elapsed-time readings quantize to ~10 ns
111	steps.
112	
113	### Why framing wobbles but loop/iter is steady
114	
115	Both constants come from the same two measurements; they
116	differ in amortization:
117	
118	- `framing = min_low - N_LOW * loop_per_iter` — inherits
119	  `min_low`'s quantization one-for-one (noise amplification
120	  ~1.01, per the comment in `src/overhead.rs`).
121	- `loop_per_iter = (min_high - min_low) / 9_900` — the same
122	  ±1-2 quanta divides by 9,900 → ±0.002 ns, invisible.
123	
124	Framing is the only quantity in the fit measured
125	un-amortized; that asymmetry is the whole story.
126	
127	### The min estimator cannot see inside a quantum
128	
129	An interval of true length T measures as ⌊T/q⌋ or ⌈T/q⌉
130	quanta depending on phase alignment; the min over many phase
131	re-rolls converges to the lower reading. So a min-based
132	estimate reports the lattice floor and can under-read the
133	true duration by up to one quantum. The true framing on the
134	3900X lies somewhere in roughly [1, 11] ns; the 1.02 and
135	21.22 readings are the floor and ceiling lattice points.
136	Within one run the phase appears stable (100k samples pick
137	one quantum); re-entering the measurement re-rolls it.
138	
139	### Error propagation through `pick_inner`
140	
141	The framing estimate is load-bearing beyond post-hoc
142	subtraction — it sizes the experiment
143	(`src/harness.rs::pick_inner`,
144	`inner ≈ 10 * framing / step_cost`):
145	
146	- Auto-sized benches: per-call adjustment error is
147	  `δ/inner ≈ δ/(10 * framing)` relative to step cost —
148	  independent of step speed. With framing ≈ 11 ns and δ up
149	  to a ~10 ns quantum, up to ~9% relative error on every
150	  auto-sized bench.
151	- Under-estimated framing under-sizes `inner`: a 1.02 ns
152	  calibration draw on a ~2.9 ns step picks inner ≈ 4 instead
153	  of ~43; the true ~11 ns framing is then ~2.8 ns per call
154	  (~50% apparatus), of which only 0.26 ns is subtracted.
155	  Nothing in the report reveals it.
156	- `--inner` override at 1 exposes the full δ (~10-20 ns)
157	  per call, unamortized.
158	
159	Consequence: a min-of-mins repeat of the current fit would
160	be the wrong fix — consistently landing on the *low* quantum
161	consistently under-sizes `inner`. Over-estimating framing is
162	harmless (bigger `inner`); under-estimating distorts.
163	
164	### Fix: amortized framing measurement
165	
166	Measure the timer-pair cost inside one window: one timer
167	read at the start, a loop of M back-to-back timer pairs, one
168	read at the end, divide by M. The ±1-quantum error on the
169	window amortizes to q/M per pair (~0.001 ns at M = 10,000) —
170	the same trick that already makes loop/iter steady.
171	
172	Caveat: this measures the *throughput* cost of paired reads,
173	which can differ from a timer pair pipelined around real
174	work. We think it is still a far better subtraction constant
175	than "somewhere in a 10 ns interval", but it carries a
176	different (small) bias, not ground truth.
177

Keep the neophyte blabbering coming — these are exactly the right questions, and one of them contains a feature idea. Three parts:

**What should n be?** Turn it around: pick n from the difference you care about. Inverting the formula, to resolve a difference Δ you need roughly **n ≈ 2·(t·s/Δ)²**. With the current statistic (s ≈ 1.2%): detecting a 2% change needs n≈4–5; a 1% change needs n≈10–12; a 0.5% change needs n≈40. So n=5 is the practical default (resolves ~1.8%), and improving the *statistic* (trimmed p10–p90, s ≈ 0.2%) is worth more than any affordable increase in n — it makes a 0.5% change detectable with n=5 instead of 40.

**Can the tool provide the LSC? Yes — but only from repeated runs, and that's a good feature.** Something like `iiac-perf tp-pc --runs 5`: run the bench n times in one invocation, compute the per-run statistic, and report `mean ± CI` and the LSC directly, so the user never touches a t-table. What the tool *cannot* honestly do is report an LSC from one run: a single run can't observe between-run variance by definition. Its internal error bar (stdev/√10M samples ≈ 0.4 ns) understates the true 58 ns run-to-run spread by two orders of magnitude — reporting that as an LSC would be a lie with confident formatting.

**Does a longer run substitute for more runs? Your own data says no** — and that's the key intuition to break. Your -d series means at 50 / 60 / 100 s were 4834 / 4726 / 4863 ns: the 100 s runs wobble exactly as much as the 5 s runs. That's because the dominant variance is *per-invocation systematic state* — which thread placement the scheduler picked, the frequency regime, the run's mode mix — and a longer run just averages longer over the *same* draw of those. More runs re-roll the draws; a longer run doesn't. (Pinning and the `performance` governor remove some of those draws, which shrinks s — that's the legitimate version of what you're reaching for.)

**Dithering's role here is real but bounded.** Within a run, the stuck lattice phase shifts *all* samples coherently by up to ±10 ns — that's a genuine run-to-run variance component, and dithering erases it. On tp-pc that's ≤10 ns of the 58 ns spread (~minor). But on fast benches — `min-now` at 24 ns/call, probes at `inner=1` where the quantum is 40% of the value — dithering is the difference between a meaningless mean and a sub-quantum one. So: dithering improves *within-run accuracy*, especially for fast paths; it cannot see mode mix or placement, so it doesn't rescue the single-run LSC.

Capturing the n-choice rule, the single-run caveat, and the `--runs` feature idea:

content.text:
That's the natural next step, and it's a good one — you've just invented **within-invocation replication**: use the OS sleeps to chop one invocation into Y statistically-separated blocks, then feed Y into the LSC formula as the replication count. Assessment of what works and what needs care:

**What a random ms-scale sleep actually re-rolls:**

- **Clock phase** — yes (the spin dither already covers this at finer grain).
- **Mode mix** — this is the big win, and I think you're right about it. The closed-loop mode mix looks like a semi-stable attractor: once producer/consumer fall into a rhythm, they stay in it — that's why it's *between*-run variance today. A sleep by one thread breaks the rhythm and re-rolls which attractor the loop lands in. That converts the dominant hidden variance component into something Y blocks can *observe*.
- **Thread placement** — partially. On an idle box the scheduler's wake-affinity usually puts a thread back on its cache-hot core, so short sleeps re-roll placement only weakly. (Pinning makes this moot anyway.)
- **Not re-rolled**: anything fixed at process start — memory layout/ASLR, the calibration draw (cached constants fix that regardless), the binary's placement. So between-block variance will still somewhat understate true between-invocation variance — worth measuring, not assuming.

**Two mechanics to get right:**

- **Post-wake warm-up discard.** Each wake pays a frequency ramp and cache refill — the first samples after a sleep are contaminated (that's the cold-calibration effect we measured). Each block needs a short discarded warm-up, or the sleeps *inject* variance instead of sampling it.
- **Randomize the sleep length** (your instinct was right) so block boundaries don't phase-lock with kernel timer ticks or the workload's own periodicity.

**Statistics:** Y blocks → per-block statistic → treat as n=Y in the LSC formula (df = 2Y−2). And it needs one honest validation experiment before we trust it: run ~10 invocations × Y=10 blocks and compare between-block to between-invocation variance (a simple ANOVA). If they're close, single-invocation LSC is real; if blocks understate, the report should say so or blend both.

**The payoff move this unlocks:** once blocks exist, an A/B mode can *interleave implementations block-by-block within one invocation* — A,B,A,B with sleeps between — and analyze *paired block differences*. Pairing cancels common-mode drift (thermal, ambient load) and typically tightens the LSC well beyond what unpaired runs achieve. That's the same reason `hyperfine` alternates commands. It would subsume `--runs n` almost entirely.

Capturing this as a design.md subsection under the LSC section and upgrading the Ideas entry:
